title: Sell Mineral Rights in Glasscock County, TX/NM
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Glasscock County, TX | Royalty Buyer
metaDescription: Glasscock County is dead center in the Midland Basin's core. A retired operations engineer explains how royalty and mineral interests here get valued.
heroLead: If you drew a bullseye on the Midland Basin, Glasscock County would sit close to the middle of it, and that geography shapes almost everything about how minerals here get priced.
intro: Glasscock County has one of the lowest populations of any county in Texas, but per square mile it's one of the most heavily drilled counties in the entire Permian Basin. Garden City, the county seat, is barely a town, yet the Wolfcamp and Spraberry acreage surrounding it has supported some of the densest multi-well pad development I've seen in twenty-plus years around this business.

That combination, tiny population, massive drilling density, means a lot of mineral owners here inherited an interest from family land that's now sitting under some of the most competitively developed acreage in Texas without ever having set foot on it themselves. If that's you, I want to make sure you understand what your interest is actually worth before you decide anything.

sections.heading: Small county, enormous drilling density
paragraphs: Glasscock County's population has stayed under two thousand for decades, but its permit counts and well density regularly rank among the top counties in the entire Permian Basin. Multiple large public operators run dense stacked-lateral programs across much of the county, targeting several Wolfcamp benches plus the Spraberry above them on the same sections.

That density is exactly why I treat Glasscock County minerals with a different level of attention than a comparably sized but lightly drilled county elsewhere in the basin. A single section here can carry a dozen or more producing horizontal wells across stacked zones, and your royalty decimal might touch several of them at once.

sections.heading: Stacked-lateral development changes the math
paragraphs: When multiple operators are developing several benches on the same acreage, your royalty check can reflect production from wells landed at very different depths and drilled years apart, each on its own decline curve. That makes a simple 'multiply the current check by X' approach almost useless here, because the blended number hides what's actually happening well by well.

I pull the specific well history tied to your unit before I build an offer, looking at how many horizons are currently producing, how recently the newest ones came online, and whether there's still room for additional development on the same acreage. That's the difference between a real number and a guess.

sections.heading: What actually sets value on your interest
paragraphs: Net royalty acres, current production across all producing horizons on your unit, overall decline trajectory, and remaining undrilled locations on the same acreage are the core inputs. Given how much of Glasscock County is already under active development, remaining undrilled locations often carry real weight rather than pure speculation, since the operators here have shown a consistent pattern of returning to fully develop acreage they've already permitted.
Values still vary with commodity pricing and the specific development stage of your unit, so I build a range off your actual documentation rather than quoting a flat number for the whole county.

sections.heading: Ranch families and inherited fractions
paragraphs: Almost all of Glasscock County's private land traces back to a handful of large historic ranching families, and mineral ownership has fractionalized across generations the way it does everywhere land like this gets passed down. It's common for me to buy from an heir who holds a small decimal interest and has never lived anywhere near the county.

I'm not a licensed appraiser, attorney, or CPA, and for questions about how a sale affects your estate or taxes, talk to your own advisor. What I offer is a direct look at your specific interest and a written offer with no pressure to accept it.

sections.heading: What to send me first
paragraphs: A recent division order or check stub is the single most useful document, since it tells me the operator, the unit, and your decimal interest directly. If you're working from an old lease or a name in a probate file instead, that's still enough to start, and I'll cross-reference it against Texas Railroad Commission production records for the relevant sections.

I'll walk you through exactly how I arrived at any number I give you, well by well if that's what it takes, because given how many horizons can be producing under a single Glasscock County section, a vague explanation isn't good enough for either of us.

faqs.question: Why does Glasscock County have so much drilling for such a small population?
faqs.answer: The county sits in the core of the Midland Basin with thick, stacked Wolfcamp and Spraberry pay, which supports dense multi-well pad development regardless of how few people live there. Well density and population aren't connected in a rural oilfield county like this one.

faqs.question: My royalty check seems to come from more than one well, is that normal here?
faqs.answer: Very common. Stacked-lateral development means multiple horizons under the same acreage can be producing at once, sometimes drilled years apart. I break down the well-by-well history before valuing your interest rather than treating the blended check as one number.

faqs.question: Is there still room for new drilling on already-developed Glasscock County acreage?
faqs.answer: Often yes. Operators here have consistently come back to fully develop acreage across multiple benches rather than drilling once and moving on, which is part of why undrilled locations on already-active units carry real weight in valuation.

faqs.question: I inherited a small fractional interest and never lived near Glasscock County, can you still help?
faqs.answer: Yes, that's an extremely common situation here given how the land has passed through generations of a handful of ranching families. Send me your division order or check stub and I'll take it from there.
